title: Spione
byline: Silent spy thriller by Fritz Lang (Fritz Lang-Film GmbH / UFA, Germany, 1928); original screenplay by Lang and Thea von Harbou.

evidence.note: Published 1928. US copyright for pre-1978 works has a maximum term of 95 years from publication (28-year initial term plus up to 67-year renewal term under the Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act). A 1928 publication's copyright expired January 1, 2024. As of September 2026 the print is in the US public domain by term.
evidence.source: US Copyright Office — How Long Does Copyright Protection Last?

evidence.note: Spione is a German production (Fritz Lang-Film GmbH, distributed by UFA) and not a US work. Under the URAA (1994), foreign works that entered US public domain due to failure of formalities could have copyright restored if still protected in their source country on January 1, 1996. Fritz Lang died August 2, 1976; Germany's life-plus-70-years term therefore runs until 2046, so the film was protected in Germany on the URAA reference date and restoration could have applied. However, URAA restoration cannot extend a work's US term beyond the statutory maximum. For a 1928 publication the ceiling is 95 years from first publication, expiring January 1, 2024. The print is in the US public domain regardless of whether URAA restoration ever applied.
evidence.source: Duke Law Center for the Study of the Public Domain — Public Domain Day 2024

evidence.note: Spione is a silent film and carried no original recorded soundtrack. All commercially circulating versions are accompanied by modern commissioned scores: Neil Brand composed the score on the Kino Lorber Blu-ray release; Donald Sosin composed the score on the Kino Lorber DVD release. Both are independently copyrighted compositions and sound recordings tied to the 2004 Murnau Stiftung restoration. The underlying 1928 imagery is in the public domain; any modern musical accompaniment attached to a specific print is separately protected.

The screenplay is an original work written in 1928 by Fritz Lang and Thea von Harbou for the film — it was not adapted from any prior published work. Thea von Harbou's novel of the same title appeared in 1929, after the film's release, making it a novelization rather than a source text. As an original 1928 work, the screenplay's US copyright expired January 1, 2024 (1928 + 95-year maximum term).
evidence.source: US Copyright Office — How Long Does Copyright Protection Last?

evidence.note: A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.

The Friedrich-Wilhelm-Murnau-Stiftung completed a 2004 digital restoration of Spione, sourced from surviving nitrate prints — the original negative no longer exists. The restored version is distributed on Blu-ray and DVD by Kino Lorber in the US (Blu-ray score: Neil Brand; DVD score: Donald Sosin) and on Blu-ray by Eureka Video (Masters of Cinema) in the UK. As a newly assembled, color-graded, digitally cleaned compilation of archival materials, the restoration constitutes a separately copyrightable work. The commissioned scores on each edition are additionally protected as independent compositions and sound recordings.
evidence.source: CriterionCast — Scott Reviews Fritz Lang's Spione [Masters of Cinema Blu-ray Review]

editorial:
Spione — released in the United States as Spies — is a 1928 German silent espionage thriller directed by Fritz Lang, the first film produced by his own company, Fritz Lang-Film GmbH, and distributed by UFA. Rudolf Klein-Rogge plays Haghi, a wheelchair-using banking magnate who secretly commands a global spy network; Willy Fritsch plays the German counter-intelligence agent sent to stop him. The film is regularly cited as a foundational prototype of the spy genre, establishing conventions — the criminal mastermind hiding behind a legitimate public identity, double agents, the ticking-clock finale — that would recur across decades of successors. The screenplay was an original work by Lang and his then-wife Thea von Harbou; her novel of the same name appeared in 1929 only after the film was already in release, making it a novelization rather than a source text.

The 1928 print and the original story are both in the US public domain by term — the maximum 95-year copyright for a 1928 publication expired January 1, 2024. Spione is a German production and could in principle have been subject to URAA restoration (Fritz Lang died in 1976, so German protection runs until 2046, and the film was still protected there on the 1996 URAA reference date), but URAA restoration cannot push a 1928 work's US term past its 95-year ceiling, which has now elapsed. The practical rights consideration for creators involves the 2004 digital restoration by the Friedrich-Wilhelm-Murnau-Stiftung, which is the primary version in commercial circulation — released by Kino Lorber on Blu-ray with a Neil Brand score and on DVD with a Donald Sosin score, and by Eureka Video (Masters of Cinema) in the UK. The restoration itself, as a faithful reproduction of public-domain footage, adds no new US copyright under Bridgeman v. Corel and Feist v. Rural; the 1928 imagery is as free in its restored form as in any earlier print. What the restoration adds can be protected: each commissioned score is an independently protected composition and sound recording, and ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD to access the footage can violate the DMCA's anti-circumvention provisions even though the underlying film is public domain.
faq: The Kino Lorber Blu-ray says 'Restored Authorized Edition' — can I use footage from it?

Not directly from the disc. The 2004 Murnau Stiftung restoration adds no new US copyright to the 1928 imagery — a faithful reproduction of public-domain footage is itself in the public domain under Bridgeman v. Corel and Feist v. Rural, so the underlying footage remains free. The Neil Brand score on the Blu-ray, however, is an independently copyrighted composition and sound recording, and ripping a copy-protected disc to extract footage can violate the DMCA's anti-circumvention provisions even though the film is public domain. Source a silent print or a provenance-verified copy for the imagery, and address the score separately if you need it.
Thea von Harbou co-wrote the screenplay — does her estate control the underlying story?

No. Von Harbou and Fritz Lang wrote the screenplay as an original work in 1928 for the film itself; her novel of the same title appeared in 1929 only after the film was already in release, so the film was not adapted from a prior published work. As an original 1928 work, the screenplay's US copyright expired January 1, 2024, and no estate claim survives on the story layer.
